paper.title: Do As I Can, Not As I Say: Grounding Language in Robotic Affordances
paper.central_claim: SayCan grounds the rich semantic knowledge of a large language model in learned robotic affordances, enabling a mobile manipulator to execute temporally extended abstract natural-language instructions in a real kitchen, with substantially higher performance than ungrounded baselines.

patterns/main/observe_act_interface.md: - **Extra tools are optional and checked per backbone.** Tools are added beside primitives rather than replacing them, harness parse/coordinate/feedback correctness is verified before comparison, and effects are reported per model: optional hybrid tools raise the strongest model 82.3 -> 85.7 SR at 0.59x calls, while imposed waypoints lift weak models (5 -> 43 SR) and move strong ones by <=2 points (2607.26148#s2, 2608.03327#s1).

- **E01 (ablation, common_practice).** Hold the frontier backbone fixed and compare the proposed harness with at least one alternative harness or loop organization on the same episodes. For zero-shot VLN-CE the alternative is a rerun of a published zero-shot harness or workflow (2606.10577#s4, 2609.15195#s4) with the same model; for coding agents, a second deployable harness. — _applies when_ a claim that a harness (rather than the model) raises embodied or agentic success.

- **E02 (ablation, common_practice).** Attribute a gain to a harness component only through one-at-a-time toggles (leave-one-out or single add) with the backbone fixed. A cumulative stack (A, then +B, then +C) or a bundle-level comparison does not separate components or their interactions. — _applies when_ a claim that a specific harness component (depth tool, memory, verifier, skill library, plugin, feedback channel) causes the improvement.

- **E03 (ablation, common_practice).** Report the harness or tool effect under at least two backbones of different strength. Several read papers find that tools and imposed structure help weak models and are neutral or harmful for strong ones. A gain measured on the teacher therefore does not predict the gain for a compact student. — _applies when_ a claim that a harness component or tool helps in general, or that a teacher-measured tool value will carry to a student.

- **E05 (metric, common_practice).** Report cost alongside success: model calls, input and output tokens, wall-clock or per-call latency, and USD per episode or per solved task, including failed trials. Harnesses with similar pass rates can differ about 40x in tokens per solved task. — _applies when_ a claim that a harness, interface or distilled student is better or more practical than an alternative.

- **E06 (dataset, common_practice).** For a VLN-CE harness, report SR, SPL, OSR and NE on R2R-CE val_unseen, either on the shared 100-episode zero-shot subset or the full split. State which one, and do not mix subset results with full-split numbers of trained methods as if they were matched. — _applies when_ an empirical claim about a zero-shot or harness-based VLN-CE / ObjectNav agent.

- **E08 (reproducibility, common_practice).** State contamination and development-overlap caveats. Frontier 'zero-shot' describes how the model was used, not what it was trained on. Disclose whether the evaluation tasks were used during harness development, and whether ablations ran under a privileged action space that is not comparable to the benchmark protocol. — _applies when_ a benchmark claim by a frontier-model harness, or ablations run under non-standard execution.

- **E16 (metric, common_practice).** Break failures down by endpoint as well as SR: never reached vs reached but wrong stop (the OSR-SR gap), false completion declarations, stuck or no-progress runs, and per-task repeat patterns. Stopping is the dominant residual failure in the read navigation papers. — _applies when_ an embodied navigation or manipulation agent's success claim, especially one that adds a stop or completion check.

- **E20 (other, common_practice).** State the depth assumption behind depth-based perception tools (pixel depth queries, back-projection, stop checks): whether depth is metric and calibrated, and whether behaviour under non-metric or scene-dependent depth was tested. — _applies when_ a harness whose tools or gates convert depth readings into distances, targets or stop decisions.

- **E22 (reproducibility, common_practice).** Compare interfaces and harnesses at a matched interaction budget: the same caps on LLM calls, turns, wall-clock time and GPU. Disclose any asymmetry, such as uncapped turns or extra compute for tool runs, because budget endings drive many success differences. — _applies when_ a comparison between harnesses, interfaces or tool bundles with the model fixed.

research/reference/researchstudio-15-31/: - **Run an ablation that isolates the conditioning signal — comparing instruction, format, or retrieval conditioning against the same multitask training without it — to prove the gain comes from conditioning and not merely from broader exposure.** _(source: both)_

- **Provide a contamination or data-overlap analysis between the adaptation tasks and the held-out evaluation set before any genuine held-out or zero-shot generalization claim is accepted.** _(source: both)_

- **Compare against the obvious cheaper alternative — longer input context, nearest-neighbor lookup, or plain multitask fine-tuning — so the unique value of the conditioning or retrieval is established rather than assumed.** _(source: reject_reviews)_

- **Justify each component of a multi-module conditioning pipeline with ablations that isolate its contribution; shallow ablations over interacting components are treated as insufficient.** _(source: both)_
- **Demonstrate that the recipe is generic across multiple tasks or domains and explain how the conditioning signal is obtained without a manual, per-task search.** _(source: reject_reviews)_

- **Characterize sensitivity to the quality and coverage of the conditioning source — the demonstration or retrieval database — and to the distributional gap between that source and the test domain.** _(source: both)_
- **Report the cost of the added structure — token and API budget, number of model or solver calls, and solver latency — rather than only end-task accuracy.** _(source: both)_

- **Provide ablations that isolate each component's marginal contribution, and especially show the claimed load-bearing step is what drives the gains rather than extra data or compute.** _(source: both)_
- **Disclose the exact prompts and implementation details so the decomposed pipeline is reproducible and the results are not suspected prompt-engineering artifacts.** _(source: both)_
- **Demonstrate generalization beyond a single narrow benchmark or domain, ideally with cross-domain or real-world tasks rather than templates specific to one dataset.** _(source: both)_
- **Compare fairly against simpler unified or end-to-end baselines and against concurrent decomposition methods, clarifying precisely what is novel relative to them.** _(source: both)_

- **Justify that the decomposition targets a genuine structural bottleneck — ideally evidenced by an empirical diagnostic linking a sub-task to the final outcome — instead of imposing structure for its own sake.** _(source: both)_

evidence.quote: We evaluate the proposed approach on 101 real-world robotic tasks
evidence.support_explanation: The system makes an embodied execution claim, not just a textual planning claim.

evidence.quote: In the mock kitchen, PaLM-SayCan achieved a planning success rate of 84% and an execution rate of 74%.
evidence.support_explanation: Planning and physical execution are separate outcomes.

evidence.quote: We find a reduction of planning performance by 3% and execution by 14%
evidence.support_explanation: Real-kitchen results correspond to81% planning and60% execution, not the mock-kitchen74% rate.

evidence.locator: Section 5, failure analysis; local text L21
evidence.quote: Overall, 65% of the errors were LLM failures and 35% were affordance failures.
evidence.support_explanation: Failure attribution is reported, though no repeated-run uncertainty accompanies this division.

evidence.quote: The RL model is trained using 16 TPUv3 chips and for about 100 hours
evidence.support_explanation: Nontrivial affordance training cost is explicit.

evidence.quote: Models whose per-skill performance outperforms prior models are ”graduated” to the same evaluation protocol in the real kitchen, and then integrated into SayCan.
evidence.support_explanation: Real-kitchen evaluation participates in skill development; it is not demonstrably construction-unseen transfer.
Termination uses a calibrated fixed heuristic affordance, not an independent task-completion verifier.

evidence.quote: involved 17 examples and recovered 88% of the solutions correctly.
evidence.support_explanation: Prompt optimization is part of system construction.

evidence.quote: If two out of the three raters agree that the skill was accomplished successfully, the episode is labelled with a positive reward.
evidence.support_explanation: Human agreement is used for skill outcome labels; high-level planning/execution success criteria are separately described in Section 5.

evidence.quote: Grounding the LLM in the real-world via affordances nearly doubles the performance over the non-grounded baselines.
evidence.support_explanation: Preserves the broad author improvement claim to be checked against the narrower planning and execution tables.

evidence.quote: We mark an execution successful if 2 out of 3 raters agree that it is successful.
evidence.support_explanation: Explicit physical task-completion judgement; separate from training labels and plan validity.

evidence.quote: The No VF and Generative approaches performed similarly, achieving 67% and 74% planning success rate respectively
evidence.support_explanation: Grounding controls measure planning; do not substitute these rates for physical execution controls.

signatures.object: Unconstrained natural-language plan versus affordance-weighted next-skill choice
signatures.information: PaLM540B prompt and completed skill labels; state-dependent RL value estimates for a bounded language-labelled skill library. Navigation has known locations; placing is scripted.
signatures.operation: Score each candidate skill for linguistic usefulness and executability; multiply the probabilities, select the maximum, execute, append its label and repeat.
signatures.output: A sequence of BC/scripted manipulation and navigation calls ending in done.
signatures.conditions: Values calibrated across heterogeneous skill types; low-level policies must implement skill semantics.
signatures.feedback: Current-state value functions affect ranking; selected labels enter history, but the high-level LLM is not given explicit execution success/failure.
signatures.selection_rule/data: Argmax LLM-probability×affordance; heuristic constant affordances for place/done and suppression of completed skills;17 few-shot prompt examples.
signatures.persistence: Static harness design and per-episode context; no accepted cross-task optimizer change is claimed.
signatures.later_use: Fixed components are reused on tasks; within-episode context is read by subsequent planner calls. This is not measured retained self-improvement.
signatures.failure_boundary: Premature termination, negation, reference ambiguity and erroneous affordance estimates.

signatures.object: Uncalibrated learned skill affordances versus comparable ranking scores
signatures.information: BC demonstrations, RL simulation rollouts and per-skill human-labelled successes; scripted navigation distances and known location information.
signatures.operation: Train value functions and skill policies, calibrate scores then combine them with LLM scores.
signatures.output: Fixed learned affordance and policy library deployed by the static harness.
signatures.conditions: Large task-specific collection/training infrastructure; availability is not a zero-data robot.
signatures.feedback: Training rewards and development evaluations, not online retained harness optimization.
signatures.selection_rule/data: Skill models graduate through mock and actual kitchen evaluation.
signatures.persistence: Static harness design and per-episode context; no accepted cross-task optimizer change is claimed.
signatures.later_use: Fixed components are reused on tasks; within-episode context is read by subsequent planner calls. This is not measured retained self-improvement.
signatures.claimed_effect: Turn linguistic usefulness into physically feasible skill selection.
signatures.failure_boundary: Selection on real-kitchen skill performance weakens unseen-deployment interpretation; placing/done use different score semantics.

gap.author_gap: LLMs know what actions make sense but not what the particular robot can do now.
gap.checked_gap: Grounded skill selection addresses semantic plans that ignore embodied capability; textual planning success and real policy execution remain distinct.

lineage/closest_adjacent.method: Language-model prompting plus BC-Z/MT-Opt skills and RL value functions.

gap.stakes: Abstract instructions cannot be completed simply by emitting plausible steps.
gap.method_response: Factor useful-in-context and executable-now scores over the same skill labels.
gap.remaining_gap: Does not resolve high-level failure-aware replanning, unreliable values, costly skill training or unpriced heuristic/known-location channels.
unresolved: Original versions of BC-Z/MT-Opt are author-described rather than independently fixed.

claims.text: SayCan grounds the rich semantic knowledge of a large language model in learned robotic affordances, enabling a mobile manipulator to execute temporally extended abstract natural-language instructions in a real kitchen, with substantially higher performance than ungrounded baselines.
claims.setting: PaLM540B; Everyday Robots mobile manipulator;15 objects,5 locations;101 instructions over7 families.
claims.baseline/control: No-VF67% planning; generative74% planning; their execution outcomes not supplied. FLAN70%/61% versus PaLM84%/74%.
claims.selection_vs_test: Prompt optimized with illustrative instruction simulator; models graduate through real kitchen skill evaluation.
claims.result/denominator: Mock84% planning/74% execution; real81%/60%; family results and101 instruction task list, not full per-task repeated outcomes.
claims.counterevidence: The abstract nearly-doubles claim is not a clean same-task executed comparison with every grounding baseline. Human-labelled criteria and trained skills remain necessary.
claims.allowed_conclusion: Author reports counted physical execution for this kitchen skill library and gains in grounded planning; not general autonomous kitchen competence or cleanly doubled physical success.

claims.text: Affordances ground useful language plans in what the robot can execute.
claims.setting: Learned RL values, BC skills and scripted skill-specific affordances.
claims.baseline/control: No-value-function planning control; human-labelled skill outcomes.
claims.selection_vs_test: Skill calibration and development evaluations are part of construction.
claims.result/denominator: 65% of residual errors attributed to LLM and35% to affordance; done score0.1.
claims.counterevidence: Values are not guarantees and selected labels do not tell the LLM whether the last skill actually worked.
claims.allowed_conclusion: A concrete state-dependent selection mechanism, with measurable but incomplete reliability.

assessment.strongest_supported_claim: Author-reported robot trials support a useful static affordance-weighted skill-selection harness in the specified kitchens. The data do not establish broadly autonomous transfer or that every ungrounded baseline suffers the claimed proportional loss in physical execution.
unresolved: Per-instruction repeated outcomes, variance and complete execution controls.
Construction-unseen test after kitchen model graduation.
assessment.reproduction: No reproduction or paper-code execution was performed.

G.reason: A specific semantic-usefulness versus current robot-capability gap is documented; closest component predecessors are described but their primary versions are not all fixed.

M.reason: Shared skill labels make product-of-scores selection reconstructible and targeted; probability calibration/independence, heuristic place/done scores and implicit state feedback leave assumptions.

X.reason: Policy/value training, calibration, skill handoff and termination are described, including known-location/scripted channels; failure-aware feedback is not part of the claimed static system and is not invented.

measurement.reason: Physical execution rates and human criteria are supplied with overall/family counts; complete repeated per-instruction success tables/verifier error audit are not. This matches the v2 partial-denominator anchor.

causality.reason: Grounding/backbone controls exist, but strongest No-VF/generative controls are planning-only, so skill capability and full executed-loop benefits are not fully separated.

holdout.reason: Mock-to-real results show deployment variation, but real-kitchen per-skill evaluations are used to graduate models; this is not construction-unseen transfer.

statistics.reason: 101 instructions and failure-cause proportions are readable, but no repeated per-task trials, CIs or seed variance substantiate precision of overall gains. Full Sections5/Appendices D–E were inspected.

cost.reason: Substantial training resources and fixed candidate-scoring structure allow partial budget reconstruction, but online token/time/USD totals and heuristic/known-location channels are not priced.

reason: Complete methods/results/Appendices A–E reviewed. Online evidence supports the scoped kitchen harness, not a construction-unseen transfer label; partial denominators and missing executed controls limit E. Provisional production-under-anchors-v2 only.
